meaning: Shows that a range reaches all the way to an extreme or very small point, stressing “even down to ...”. It can also mean something has continued up to a certain time.
connection: Noun + に至るまで (often 「〜から〜に至るまで」)

senses.label: Range reaching to ...
senses.meaning: Names a start and an end point to stress how wide the range is. The end point is often something surprising or very small. Like “from A all the way to B” or “even down to B”.
senses.connection: Noun A + から + Noun B + に至るまで (often followed by 「すべて」, 「幅広く」, 「まで」)
examples: It is loved by every generation, from children to the elderly.
I was strictly coached on everything, from my clothes down to the way I spoke.
In this hotel, everything from the furniture to the tableware is handmade by craftsmen.

senses.label: Continuing up to a time
senses.meaning: Shows that a state has continued from the past up to a certain point in time. Written style. Often used with 「今日」 or 「現在」.
senses.connection: Time noun + に至るまで (e.g. 「今日に至るまで」, 「現在に至るまで」)
examples: The truth about the incident remains unknown to this day.
From our founding to the present day, we have always put quality first.

notes: Dropping 「まで」 changes the meaning completely: 「死に至る病」 is “a disease that leads to death”, while 「死に至るまで働いた」 means “worked right up until death”. On its own, 「に至る」 means “end up in / reach (a result)”, whereas 「に至るまで」 means a range or period stretches all the way to a point.

Don't use it for a plain start and end time; it sounds overblown. ✕「月曜日から水曜日に至るまで休みです」→ ○「月曜日から水曜日まで休みです」. The end point should be the farthest or smallest item, the one that makes you think “even that?”.
After 「今日に至るまで」 and 「現在に至るまで」 use a continuing state or a negative, not a one-off action: ✕「今日に至るまで結婚した」→ ○「今日に至るまで独身を通している」.

daily.title: Praising a restaurant
daily.description: Telling a friend about a restaurant that is very particular.
daily.example: That place is really particular about everything, from the ingredients to the dishes.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A news report on how widespread a trend is.
daily.example: Everyone from elementary school kids to adults is hooked on this anime.

work.title: Company profile
work.description: Describing the company's history on its website or in a brochure.
work.example: Since our founding, and to this very day, we have grown together with our local community.

work.title: Checking work
work.description: A boss asks a team member to double-check some documents.
work.example: Please check everything again carefully, from the figures down to any typos.

etymology: 「至る」 originally means “to arrive, to reach”. Combined with 「まで」 (end point), it literally means “all the way until reaching ...”. This led to the meaning “a range extending to a certain end point”.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning. 「から〜まで」 just states a start and an end point neutrally, while 「から〜に至るまで」 stresses how far or how small the end point is, with a tone of “even ...!”. In conversation 「から〜まで」 is enough; 「に至るまで」 appears mostly in writing, advertising and speeches.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both can show a wide range. 「にわたって」 looks at the length and breadth of the whole span and usually follows a period or area (「3日間にわたって」); 「に至るまで」 looks at the end point and often lists both ends as 「AからBに至るまで」.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: They share the same origin (both come from 「至る」). 「に至る／に至って」 says a situation finally developed to some serious stage (「倒産に至る」); 「に至るまで」 says a range or period extends to a point, with the focus on thorough coverage.

similar.title: 〜に至っては
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「に至っては」 picks the most extreme example after a list and comments on it, usually negatively (「弟に至っては一度も来ない」). 「に至るまで」 only says the range reaches that end and is neutral in itself.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (the point reached) + the verb 「至る」 (to reach) + 「まで」 (the limit). 「至る」 already means “to go all the way to the end”, and adding 「まで」 stresses the end point twice: “right up to the very end”. That pushes the end item to the farthest, smallest or most unexpected position and gives the feeling of “even ...”. It is often written 「AからBに至るまで」, naming both ends to show how wide the coverage is. When the end point is a time word such as 「今日」 or 「現在」, it means a state has continued all the way to the present. 「至る」 is a Sino-Japanese, written-style verb, so the whole phrase sounds more formal than plain 「まで」.

meaning: Uses something as an excuse or cover for doing what you really want to do. It carries criticism, or self-mockery when said about yourself.

senses.label: Using ... as an excuse
senses.meaning: The stated reason is the first part, but the real goal is the second. Like “using ... as an excuse” or “under the pretext of ...”. Usually critical, but can also be self-mocking.
senses.connection: Noun + にかこつけて + action (e.g. 「出張にかこつけて」, 「仕事にかこつけて」, 「病気にかこつけて」)
examples: Using a business trip as an excuse, I enjoyed a hot-spring getaway.
He uses work as an excuse to leave all the housework to his wife.
I used the rain as an excuse to skip my jog.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜にかこつけた + noun」 describes a noun as “... done under the pretext of ...”. The criticism is stronger here.
senses.connection: Noun + にかこつけた + Noun
examples: Customers complained about the price increase made under the pretext of an anniversary.
Overseas trips disguised as inspection tours have become a problem.

notes: It carries a negative nuance of “using X as a pretext”. Said about someone else, it accuses them of impure motives; telling a boss or client 「出張にかこつけて観光なさったんですね」 is very rude. About yourself, it is self-mocking.
Once the first part takes 「かこつけて」, it becomes a “borrowed excuse” and the meaning shifts: 「病気にかこつけて会社を休んだ」 implies taking the day off on the pretext of illness. For real illness, say 「病気で会社を休んだ」.
It attaches to nouns. To use a clause, nominalize it first: ✕「雨が降ったにかこつけて」→ ○「雨にかこつけて」 or 「雨が降ったことにかこつけて」.

daily.title: Complaining among friends
daily.description: A friend complains that her husband always finds excuses to drink.
daily.example: My husband uses work socializing as an excuse to come home drunk every night.

daily.title: Mocking your own laziness
daily.description: Confessing to your family that you used an excuse to rest.
daily.example: I used my slight cold as an excuse to lounge around all day.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A report on officials traveling for fun under the name of official business.
work.example: It is drawing criticism as a sightseeing trip disguised as official business.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: A coworker teases someone who sightsees on business trips.
work.example: That guy always uses business trips as an excuse to go sightseeing.

etymology: 「かこつける」 is written 「託ける」 in kanji. It originally meant “to entrust something to, to rely on something else”. From “pinning a matter on something else” it came to mean “to use something as an excuse”.

similar.title: 〜をいいことに
similar.explanation: The meaning is close; both imply criticism of dubious motives. 「をいいことに」 means “taking advantage of a favorable situation to do what you shouldn't”, so the first part is an opportunity (「親が留守なのをいいことに」). 「にかこつけて」 means “using A as an excuse to do B”, so the first part is the reason given outwardly.

similar.title: 〜を兼ねて
similar.explanation: Both show that one act serves another purpose too. 「を兼ねて」 is open and above board, “doubling as / at the same time”, and can be said publicly (「視察を兼ねて」). 「にかこつけて」 implies the first part is only a front, with a negative or self-mocking tone.

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: 「がてら」 means “while at it”, and both actions are real purposes (「散歩がてら買い物する」). With 「にかこつけて」 the real purpose is the second action, and the first is just an excuse.

formation: It is made of the particle 「に」 (target) + the te-form of the verb 「かこつける」 (託ける: to hang one thing on another). 「AにかこつけてB」 literally means “hang B on A”: what you really want to do, B, is hung on a respectable reason, A, which stands in for it. Because it is only “hanging on”, A and B have no real connection, which naturally brings out the sense of a pretext and the speaker's sarcasm. The te-form links this “in the name of A” manner to the action B; before a noun it becomes 「にかこつけた＋noun」.

meaning: Shows that something can easily be imagined, understood, or guessed from the situation. Written style, like “it is not hard to ...”.
connection: Noun / Verb dictionary form + に難くない

senses.label: Not hard to imagine
senses.meaning: Follows a noun about thinking or understanding, meaning “easy to imagine / understand”. The most common phrase is 「想像に難くない」. Formal; seen mostly in writing and news commentary.
senses.connection: Noun + に難くない (「想像」, 「理解」, 「推測」, 「予想」, etc.)
examples: The suffering of the disaster victims is not hard to imagine.
It is easy to understand that he agonized over that decision.
It is not hard to predict that the losses will continue if nothing changes.

senses.label: Not hard to sense
senses.meaning: Follows a verb in dictionary form, usually 「察する」, meaning “it is not hard to sense how someone feels”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に難くない (mainly 「察するに難くない」)
examples: It is not hard to sense his grief at suddenly losing his family.
The parents' worry is easy to sense.

notes: It contains the negative 「ない」 but the meaning is positive: “easy to imagine”. 「想像に難くない」 is “not hard to imagine”; never read it as “hard to imagine” (that is 「想像しがたい」).
It only follows a few words of inference such as 「想像」, 「推測」, 「理解」 and 「察する」: ✕「実現に難くない」→ ○「実現は難しくない」 or 「容易に実現できる」.
It is read 「かたくない」, not ✕「がたくない」 or ✕「にくくない」.
It has the tone of an onlooker's inference. Saying it directly to the person concerned (「あなたの悲しみは想像に難くない」) sounds stiff and condescending; to comfort someone, say 「さぞお辛いことと思います」 instead.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: An editorial on the situation of residents in a disaster area.
daily.example: The hardship of life in an evacuation shelter is not hard to imagine.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the main character's state of mind.
daily.example: The loneliness of the boy who lost his mother is not hard to sense.

work.title: Analysis report
work.description: Predicting market trends in a report.
work.example: It is not hard to imagine that competition will become even fiercer.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Discussing the causes of a phenomenon.
work.example: It is not hard to infer that economic inequality affects education.

etymology: 「難い (かたい)」 is a classical adjective meaning “difficult”, sharing its origin with 「〜がたい」. 「に難くない」 literally means “it is not difficult to ...”. It comes from the style of reading classical Chinese texts in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜がたい
similar.explanation: They share the same origin (both from 「難い」). 「がたい」 attaches to the verb stem and means “hard to ...” (「信じがたい」); 「に難くない」 attaches to a noun and uses the negative to mean “not hard to ...”, and only with words of imagining or inference.

similar.title: 〜に相違ない
similar.explanation: Both express a confident inference. 「に相違ない」 is the speaker asserting “it must be ...” (「犯人は彼に相違ない」); 「に難くない」 judges that “it is easy to imagine”, and sounds more objective and indirect.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (target) + the continuative form 「難く」 of the classical adjective 「難し（かたし）」 + the negative 「ない」. 「難い」 means “difficult”, so 「難くない」 is “not difficult”: “for (imagining), it is not hard”. By denying difficulty it expresses the positive judgment that anyone can easily think of it, which is more indirect and literary than simply saying 「容易だ」. Since 「難い」 is a relic of old Japanese, it only pairs with inference words like 「想像」, 「推測」, 「理解」 or 「察する」, forming a fixed combination.

meaning: A written-style expression with several uses: “only at (a stage)”, “even someone like ...”, “in an instant”, “both A and B”, and “while remaining in a state”.

senses.label: Only at ... (finally)
senses.meaning: Shows that something finally happened only at a certain age, attempt, or stage. Stresses “it took that long / it wasn't easy”. Often used with 「初めて」, 「ようやく」, or 「やっと」.
senses.connection: Age / number / time noun + にして + 初めて・ようやく
examples: I traveled abroad for the first time at the age of fifty.
I finally passed on my third attempt.

senses.label: Even someone like ...
senses.meaning: Takes a very skilled person as an example: “if even they are like this, others certainly are”. Common patterns: 「この〜にしてこの〜」 and 「〜にしてそうなのだから」.
senses.connection: Noun for a person or level + にして + この／こんな／そう
examples: Even someone as experienced as him made this mistake.
If even a veteran like Mr. Tanaka finds it hard, it will be impossible for a newcomer.

senses.label: In an instant
senses.meaning: After words for a very short time like 「一瞬」 or 「一夜」, it means “in no time at all”. A fixed combination.
senses.connection: 一瞬・一夜・一日, etc. + にして
examples: The house was reduced to ashes in an instant by the fire.
That movie made him a star overnight.

senses.label: Both A and B
senses.meaning: Shows that someone or something has two roles or qualities at once: “both A and B”. Written and slightly literary.
senses.connection: Noun A + にして + Noun B (である／でもある); also 「最初にして最後」, etc.
examples: He is both a doctor and a novelist.
This is the first and last chance.

senses.label: While remaining as is
senses.meaning: After 「ながら」, it means “while remaining in that state”. Fixed phrases, mostly in writing.
senses.connection: 「生まれながらにして」, 「居ながらにして」
examples: All people are born equal.
Thanks to the internet, you can shop without leaving home.

notes: It differs from 「にしては」 by just one 「は」, but the meaning is entirely different: 「50歳にして初めて海外へ行った」 is “went abroad for the first time at 50”; 「50歳にしては若く見える」 is “looks young for a 50-year-old”.
The “even ...” use criticizes the result: 「部長にしてこのミスだ」 publicly blames the department head. Saying this to a superior or client is very rude; it suits only commentary or written reports.
It is written style. In daily conversation 「〜になって初めて」, 「一瞬で」 or 「一晩で」 sounds more natural; using 「にして」 often in speech sounds stiff and affected.
In the “both roles” use, A and B are both nouns showing two identities of the same person or thing: ✕「医者にして優しい」→ ○「医者にして小説家」.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A report on an elderly woman achieving her dream.
daily.example: She graduated from university for the first time at the age of eighty.

daily.title: Amazed at fast change
daily.description: Friends talk about an influencer who suddenly became famous.
daily.example: That person became famous overnight, huh.

daily.title: Watching sports
daily.description: A commentator remarks on a star athlete's mistake.
daily.example: Such a result, even from a world champion — that's surprising.

work.title: Introducing a guest
work.description: Introducing the guest speaker at a lecture.
work.example: Today's speaker is Professor Yamada, who is both a researcher and a business owner.

work.title: Explaining a service
work.description: Explaining how convenient an online service is.
work.example: With this service, you can view properties across the country without leaving your office.

etymology: Made of the particle 「に」, 「し」 (the stem of 「する」), and the particle 「て」. It continues classical expressions like 「にて」 that marked status, state, or a point in time, which is why it sounds very formal.

similar.title: 〜て初めて
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「て初めて」 follows the te-form and means you realize something only after experiencing it (「親になって初めて分かった」); 「にして初めて」 follows nouns like an age or count and stresses that something was achieved only at that stage; it is more formal.

similar.title: 〜にしてからが
similar.explanation: Same origin, and close to the “even ...” sense. 「にしてからが」 gives a typical example to criticize: “even X does this, let alone others” (「社長にしてからが遅刻する」). The “even ...” of 「にして」 means “even someone this capable ...”, with the focus on surprise.

similar.title: 〜でもあり〜でもある
similar.explanation: Both can show two roles at once. 「AにしてB」 is more formal and concise (「医者にして作家」); 「AでもありBでもある」 is more colloquial and can also take na-adjectives.

similar.title: 〜にしては
similar.explanation: Same origin (both are 「に＋して」), different meaning. 「にしては」 means “considering that it is A, surprisingly ...” (「子供にしては上手だ」); 「にして」 means “only at ...”, “even ...” and so on. With or without 「は」 the meaning is entirely different.

formation: It is built from the case particle 「に」 + the stem 「し」 of the verb 「する」 + the conjunctive particle 「て」, and corresponds to classical 「にて」. 「に」 marks a point (a time, status or state), and 「して」 means “being at that point, in that capacity”, so the core of 「AにしてB」 is “B, standing at A”. When A is an age or a count, it means “only at point A does B happen”; when A is a person, “even someone of status A does B”; when A is 「一瞬」 or 「一夜」, “in just that instant B”; when A and B are both roles, “both A and B”. Every sense grows out of “standing at A”, which is why it can only follow a noun.

meaning: Thinking, judging, or acting based on facts, reality, or rules, in line with the actual situation. Written style.
connection: Noun + に即して／に即した + Noun

senses.label: In line with reality
senses.meaning: Acting closely in line with facts, current conditions, or experience. Stresses “not losing touch with reality”. Usually written 「即して」.
senses.connection: 「事実」, 「現実」, 「実態」, 「現状」, 「状況」, etc. + に即して／に即した + Noun
examples: Please make your judgment based on the facts.
Measures suited to the current situation are needed.
It's easier to understand if you speak from your own experience.

senses.label: In accordance with rules
senses.meaning: Handling something according to laws, regulations, or customs. In this sense it is often written 「則して」. Formal.
senses.connection: 「法律」, 「規則」, 「ルール」, 「基準」, etc. + に則して
examples: We will handle this properly in accordance with the law.
Please follow the procedures set out in the company regulations.

notes: 「即して」 and 「則して」 sound the same but differ in emphasis: 「事実に即して」 is “in line with the facts”, 「法律に則して」 is “following the law”. Using the wrong kanji in formal documents looks careless.
「則して」 is read 「そくして」; 「法に則って」 is read 「のっとって」. Don't mix up the readings.
It follows objective grounds such as facts, the current situation, actual conditions or rules, not people: ✕「上司に即して行動する」→ ○「上司の指示に従って行動する」.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A report on a government policy.
daily.example: Support that fits each region's actual situation is needed.

daily.title: Discussing a problem
daily.description: A friend reminds you not to talk in the abstract.
daily.example: Let's not talk ideals — let's think about it realistically.

work.title: Meeting
work.description: A boss asks the team to make a plan based on data.
work.example: Let's redo next term's plan based on the data.

work.title: Formal notice
work.description: A company notice explains how a matter will be handled.
work.example: This matter will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the work regulations.

etymology: 「即する」 is a verb made from the Sino-Japanese word 「即」 plus 「する」. 「即」 means “close to, right next to”, so it means “to closely match”. The 「則」 in 「則する」 means “rule, law”, so it means “to take ... as a standard”.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: 「に沿って」 means “along / in accordance with (a policy, plan or expectation)” and is more common (「計画に沿って」); 「に即して」 is more literary and stresses fitting the facts or the situation.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「に基づいて」 means “on the basis of” (「データに基づいて」); 「に即して」 puts more weight on not departing from actual circumstances.

similar.title: 〜にのっとって
similar.explanation: 「にのっとって」 means following tradition, rules or etiquette, close to 「則して」; 「即して」 is mostly used with facts and the current situation.

similar.title: 〜に照らして
similar.explanation: 「に照らして」 means “judge by comparing with ...”, stressing reference and comparison (「法律に照らして判断する」); 「に即して」 means “act in step with ...”.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (basis) + the te-form of the Sino-Japanese verb 「即する」 (to stick close, not to depart from). In Chinese-origin kanji compounds 「即」 already means “close to” (as in 「不即不離」), so 「Aに即してB」 amounts to “do B sticking close to A”. When A is a fact or the present situation, it means “without departing from reality”; if 「即」 is replaced by 「則」 (rule), written 「則して」, it becomes “using the rules as the yardstick”. The te-form links the following action, and 「に即した」 modifies a noun.

meaning: Shows that something has enough value or strength to be worth doing, or can stand up to a test.
connection: Noun / Verb dictionary form + に堪える

senses.label: Worth ...
senses.meaning: Shows that the content or quality is good enough to be worth seeing or reading. A positive evaluation. Common phrases: 「鑑賞に堪える」, 「読むに堪える」.
senses.connection: Nouns like 「鑑賞」, 「観賞」 / dictionary-form verbs like 「読む」, 「見る」 + に堪える
examples: This painting is good enough to satisfy even professional viewers.
Although it is a student's work, it is a novel well worth reading.

senses.label: Able to withstand
senses.meaning: Shows that something can stand up to use, criticism, or testing without breaking down. In this sense it is often written 「耐える」.
senses.connection: Nouns like 「使用」, 「批判」, 「検証」, 「風雪」 + に堪える／に耐える
examples: I chose sturdy furniture that will hold up to years of use.
I want to do research that can stand up to criticism from experts.
This bridge is designed to withstand even a major earthquake.

notes: When you see 「堪え」, first check whether 「ない」 follows: 「見るに堪える」 is “worth looking at”, 「見るに堪えない」 is “unbearable to look at”. Overlook the negative and the meaning is reversed.
The “worth ...” sense means “reaches a standard, presentable”, not high praise. Telling a boss or client their work 「鑑賞に堪える」 sounds condescending; to praise, use 「素晴らしい」 or 「見事ですね」.
For “endure” the usual kanji is 「耐える」, and for “be worth” it is 「堪える」: 「重さに耐える」, 「鑑賞に堪える」.
「堪える」 can also be read 「こらえる」 (to hold back), as in 「涙を堪える」; in this grammar it is read 「たえる」.

daily.title: Recommending a work
daily.description: Recommending a manga by an amateur artist to a friend.
daily.example: It's an amateur's work, but it's definitely worth a look.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: Choosing a durable table at a furniture store.
daily.example: I want a table that can handle everyday use.

work.title: Research guidance
work.description: A professor sets expectations for a student's thesis.
work.example: Collect data that can withstand verification by a third party.

work.title: Product description
work.description: Explaining how durable a product is.
work.example: This product is designed to withstand use even in harsh environments.

etymology: 「堪える (たえる)」 originally means “to endure, to bear”. From “being able to bear something” it came to mean “having enough strength or value”, that is, “worth ...”.

similar.title: 〜に足る
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に足る」 stresses “sufficient, qualified” and is mostly used in 「信頼に足る」 and 「尊敬に足る」; 「に堪える」 stresses “stands up to appreciation or scrutiny” and is mostly used for works and research.

similar.title: 〜に値する
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に値する」 means “has the value of ...” and combines widely (「注目に値する」, 「称賛に値する」); 「に堪える」 has limited collocations, with the feeling of “good enough”.

similar.title: 〜に堪えない
similar.explanation: Same origin. The negative 「に堪えない」 means “unbearable to ...” or “cannot help feeling ...”, and is not simply “not worth ...”.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (target) + the verb 「堪える（たえる）」 (to withstand). 「Aに堪える」 literally means “withstand A”. When A is weight, criticism or time, it means “can stand up to it”; when A is 「鑑賞」, 「読む」 or 「見る」, it means “can withstand being appreciated or read”, that is, “of high enough quality to be worth ...”. So the “worth” sense extends from “stands up to scrutiny”, which is why it stresses “meets the standard” rather than “outstanding”.

meaning: Shows that something is so bad you can't bear to watch or listen to it, or, after an emotion noun, that a feeling is too strong to hold back.
connection: Verb dictionary form / emotion noun + に堪えない

senses.label: Unbearable to ...
senses.meaning: After 「見る」, 「聞く」, 「読む」, etc., it means something is too terrible or offensive to face. Expresses strong disgust or discomfort.
senses.connection: Dictionary-form verbs like 「見る」, 「聞く」, 「読む」 + に堪えない
examples: The accident scene was too horrible to look at.
The internet is full of abuse too vile to listen to.
This article has so many errors that it's unreadable.

senses.label: Overwhelmed with ...
senses.meaning: After a noun for an emotion, it means the feeling is so strong it can't be held back. Very formal; used mostly in speeches and letters.
senses.connection: 「感謝」, 「感激」, 「遺憾」, 「同情」, 「喜び」, etc. + (の念)に堪えない
examples: I am deeply grateful to all of you for your support.
It is truly regrettable that things have come to this.

notes: The two senses have opposite tones. After 「見る・聞く・読む」 it is strongly negative (“unbearable to see”); after feeling nouns such as 「感謝・遺憾・同情」 it is a formal “I cannot help feeling ... / deeply ...”. Put the wrong word before it and the meaning changes entirely.
「見るに堪えない」 and 「聞くに堪えない」 are very harsh, like “painful to watch, painful to hear”. Used on someone's work or speech, they are very hurtful and at work amount to rejecting everything.
「感謝に堪えません」 and 「遺憾に堪えません」 are formal set phrases for speeches and letters; with friends they sound exaggerated and stiff. To thank someone normally, 「本当にありがとう」 is enough.
For physical “can't stand it” (heat, pain) use 「耐えられない」, not this grammar: ✕「痛みに堪えない」→ ○「痛みに耐えられない」.

daily.title: Watching TV
daily.description: Complaining that variety shows are tasteless.
daily.example: A lot of variety shows these days are unbearable to watch.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: News about a politician's gaffe.
daily.example: The lawmaker's remarks were too offensive to listen to.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: A company president thanks guests at a ceremony.
work.example: I am truly moved that so many of you have gathered here today.

work.title: Apology statement
work.description: A company expresses regret over an incident in a statement.
work.example: We deeply regret the great inconvenience we have caused.

etymology: 「堪える」 means “to endure, to bear”, so the negative 「堪えない」 means “cannot bear”. “Can't bear to see or hear” gave the meaning “unbearable”, and “a feeling too strong to bear” gave “overwhelmed with”.

similar.title: 〜に堪える
similar.explanation: Same origin. The affirmative means “worth ...” or “stands up to ...”; the negative means “unbearable to ...” or “deeply ...”, and is not simply the opposite.

similar.title: 〜たものではない
similar.explanation: Close to the “unbearable” sense. 「見られたものではない」 and 「聞けたものではない」 also mean “can't bear to look / listen at all” and are more colloquial; 「見るに堪えない」 is more literary and formal.

similar.title: 〜を禁じ得ない
similar.explanation: Close to the “deeply ...” sense. 「を禁じ得ない」 means “cannot help feeling ...” (「同情を禁じ得ない」), stressing that the feeling is involuntary; 「に堪えない」 is mostly used in formal thanks and apologies.

similar.title: 〜てやまない
similar.explanation: Both show strong feeling. 「てやまない」 shows a wish or feeling that continues without stopping (「願ってやまない」); 「に堪えない」 shows a feeling so strong it is hard to bear, mostly as a speech formula.

formation: It is made of 「に」 + the negative 「堪えない」 of 「堪える」 (to withstand), literally “cannot withstand ...”. After 「見る」 or 「聞く」 it means “cannot bear to look / listen”, so the content is too awful to look at or hear; after feeling nouns like 「感謝」 or 「遺憾」 it means “cannot bear the weight of this feeling”, so the feeling overflows and is hard to contain, i.e. “deeply ...”. The same “cannot bear it” turns negative when the object is outside content and becomes a formal intensifier when the object is an inner feeling; that is how the two senses split.

meaning: Shows that something fully meets the conditions or has enough value to be worth doing. The negative means “not worth ...”.
connection: Noun (stem of a する-verb) / Verb dictionary form + に足る

senses.label: Worthy of / enough to
senses.meaning: Shows that something has enough value or qualifies. Usually modifies a noun: 「〜に足る + noun」. Written style; a high evaluation.
senses.connection: Nouns like 「信頼」, 「尊敬」, 「満足」 / dictionary-form verbs like 「信じる」, 「頼る」 + に足る (+ noun)
examples: He is a person worthy of trust.
We did not get a result good enough to be satisfied with.
There is no evidence sufficient to support that claim.

senses.label: Not worth mentioning
senses.meaning: The negatives 「〜に足らない」 and 「〜に足りない」 mean “not worth ..., trivial”. Common fixed phrases: 「取るに足らない」, 「恐るるに足らず」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に足らない／に足りない／に足らず
examples: That's a trivial problem.
The opposing team is nothing to fear.

notes: 「取るに足らない」 means “trivial”. Applied to someone else's opinion or work it is very rude; use it only humbly about your own matters (「取るに足らない話ですが」).

Don't confuse it with quantity “not enough”: 「恐れるに足らない」 is “nothing to be afraid of”, not “not enough fear”; 「時間が足りない」 is the quantity use. This grammar always has 「に」 before it, preceded by an action or evaluative word.
It follows a noun or the dictionary form of a verb: ○「信頼に足る」, 「信頼するに足る」; ✕「信頼したに足る」.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Cheering up a friend who's worried about something small.
daily.example: That's nothing worth worrying about. Don't let it bother you.

daily.title: Judging someone
daily.description: Talking with family about a new neighbor.
daily.example: I think that person can be trusted.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Pointing out a lack of evidence at a review meeting.
work.example: This report has no data sufficient to support its conclusion.

work.title: Recommending a partner
work.description: Recommending a business partner to your boss.
work.example: That company is a trustworthy business partner.

etymology: 「足る」 is an old verb with the same meaning as modern 「足りる」: “to be enough”. 「に足る」 literally means “is enough for ...”, which led to “worthy of / enough to”.

similar.title: 〜に値する
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に値する」 stresses “has the value of ...” (「注目に値する」); 「に足る」 stresses “sufficient conditions, qualified” (「信頼に足る」).

similar.title: 〜に堪える
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に堪える」 stresses “stands up to appreciation or scrutiny” (「鑑賞に堪える」); 「に足る」 stresses “enough to, qualified to”.

similar.title: 〜には当たらない
similar.explanation: Close to the negative form. 「には当たらない」 means “no need to ...” (「驚くには当たらない」); 「に足らない」 means “not worth ...” (「恐れるに足らない」). The former stresses “unnecessary”, the latter “the object is too slight”.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (target) + the classical verb 「足る」 (to be enough). 「Aに足る」 means “is enough for A”: the conditions or qualifications are sufficient for doing A, so “enough to / worth ...”. The negative 「Aに足らない」 means “falls short of A”, i.e. “not worth A”; 「取るに足らない」 is “not worth picking up and dealing with”, hence trivial. Using classical 「足る」 rather than modern 「足りる」 gives the whole expression a written, evaluative tone.

meaning: Shows that something is not limited to one area but extends further. Like “not limited to ...”.
connection: Noun / Verb plain form + にとどまらず

senses.label: Not limited to
senses.meaning: Shows that an effect or activity goes beyond the first range and spreads to a wider one. Formal; common in the news.
senses.connection: Noun / Verb dictionary form + にとどまらず、〜も／〜まで
examples: This issue is being debated not only in Japan but all over the world.
His activities are not limited to music; they extend even to film and novels.
That shop doesn't just sell products; it also holds classes on how to use them.

senses.label: Sentence end / modifying
senses.meaning: 「〜にとどまらない」 can end a sentence or modify a noun: “is not just ...”. You can also say 「〜にとどまるものではない」.
senses.connection: Noun + にとどまらない／にとどまるものではない
examples: The damage is not limited to one area.
The significance of this reform is not limited to the economy.

notes: What is denied is “staying only at the first item”; the first item itself still holds: 「国内にとどまらず」 is “not only in Japan”, not “not in Japan”.
The first item is the smaller range and the second the larger; reverse them and it makes no sense: ✕「世界にとどまらず日本でも」→ ○「日本にとどまらず世界でも」.
Here 「止まらず」 is read 「とどまらず」; read 「とまらず」 it means “can't stop” (「涙が止まらない」), a completely different meaning.

daily.title: Talking about a star
daily.description: Friends talk about a singer's popularity.
daily.example: That singer's popularity isn't limited to Japan — it's spread all over Asia.

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: News about the impact of a pandemic.
daily.example: The impact is not limited to tourism; it has reached the restaurant industry too.

work.title: Company presentation
work.description: Explaining the company's business scope at a press event.
work.example: We don't just sell products; we also put great effort into after-sales service.

work.title: Academic presentation
work.description: Discussing the significance of research.
work.example: The results of this study go beyond the field of medicine.

etymology: 「とどまる (止まる・留まる)」 means “to stay, to stop at a place”. The negative 「とどまらず」 literally means “not staying at ...”, which came to mean “not limited to ...”.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「のみならず」 means “not only ... but also ...” and stresses addition; 「にとどまらず」 stresses that the range goes beyond the first item and keeps expanding.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. After 「ばかりか」 the second item is often more serious or surprising; it is used in both speech and writing. 「にとどまらず」 is more literary and stresses the spread of range.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に限らず」 means “not limited to ..., also ...”, with the first item given as a representative example; 「にとどまらず」 stresses influence or activity spreading from a small range to a larger one.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (the range) + the negative continuative form 「とどまらず」 of the verb 「とどまる」 (to remain in a place); 「ず」 is the classical negative, equivalent to 「〜ないで」. 「Aにとどまらず」 literally means “not staying within the range of A”, which naturally leads to “and it spreads beyond”, so the second part must be a wider range, often echoed by 「も」 or 「まで」. The 「ず」 continuative is a written form; at the end of a sentence, say 「にとどまらない」 or 「にとどまるものではない」.

meaning: Contrasts two opposite things: “in contrast to ...”. Usually carries the speaker's judgment or feelings.
connection: Noun / plain form + の + にひきかえ

senses.label: In contrast to ...
senses.meaning: The two situations are complete opposites. Usually subjective, praising one side and criticizing the other.
senses.connection: Noun + にひきかえ
examples: Unlike his serious older brother, the younger one does nothing but play.
Compared to last year's scorching heat, this summer is cool.

senses.label: After a clause
senses.meaning: After a clause, use 「〜のにひきかえ」. Shows a sharp contrast between two things.
senses.connection: Verb / い-adjective plain form; な-adjective / noun + な + のにひきかえ
examples: Whereas the older sister is outgoing, the younger one is very quiet.
My previous boss was strict, but my current boss is very kind.

senses.label: As a conjunction
senses.meaning: 「それにひきかえ」 can start a sentence as a conjunction, contrasting with what came before. Also common in speech.
senses.connection: (Previous sentence). それにひきかえ、〜
examples: The neighbors' kid studies hard. Mine, on the other hand…

notes: It carries a clear value judgment and is often used to complain or mock oneself. Comparing a brother or colleague to someone to their face (「お兄さんにひきかえ、君は…」) is very hurtful and considered rude in Japan.
Before a clause, add 「の」: ✕「兄が真面目にひきかえ」→ ○「兄が真面目なのにひきかえ」.
「景品と引き換える」 and 「代金引換」 use the original meaning “exchange” and take an object; the grammar 「にひきかえ」 is followed directly by the contrasting sentence. Don't confuse them.

daily.title: A parent complains
daily.description: A mother compares her two children with a friend.
daily.example: My first child was so easy, but the second one is really a handful.

daily.title: Comparing the weather
daily.description: Chatting with family about this winter.
daily.example: Unlike last year's heavy snow, it's hardly snowed at all this year.

work.title: Sales analysis
work.description: Comparing two divisions' results at a meeting.
work.example: In contrast to our strong overseas business, domestic sales are sluggish.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: An editorial compares how two countries responded.
work.example: Unlike our neighbor, which responded swiftly, our country's measures are lagging behind.

etymology: 「ひきかえる (引き換える)」 originally means “to exchange”. From “swapping one side for the other to look at it” it came to mean “in contrast to”.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に対して」 can contrast two things objectively (「兄が文系なのに対して、弟は理系だ」); 「にひきかえ」 carries a strong subjective judgment, often praise or blame.

similar.title: 〜反面
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「反面」 mostly describes two sides of the same thing (「便利な反面、危険もある」); 「にひきかえ」 compares two different people or things.

similar.title: 〜に比べて
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「に比べて」 is an ordinary comparison and can be just a difference in degree; 「にひきかえ」 stresses that the two are sharply opposite, with a note of feeling.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (the thing compared) + the continuative form of the verb 「ひきかえる（引き換える）」 (to swap), used as a pause. 「Aにひきかえ」 literally means “swapped round with A”: put A and B in the same position and switch them, and the difference shows at once, so it means “in contrast to A”. Since swapping only makes sense when two things are sharply different, the two parts are usually opposite ends, with the speaker's exclamation or judgment. As a conjunction it is 「それにひきかえ」.

meaning: Shows that the first thing is already at a high level, and the second goes even further. With a question word, it means “more than anything”, i.e. “the most”.
connection: Noun / question word + にもまして

senses.label: Even more than ...
senses.meaning: Admits the first thing is already notable, but the second surpasses it: “even more than ...”. Often used with time nouns.
senses.connection: Noun (「以前」, 「去年」, 「前回」, 「いつ」, etc.) + にもまして
examples: This summer is even hotter than last year.
She has become even more beautiful than before.
Today he seems even more down than usual.

senses.label: More than anything
senses.meaning: After question words like 「何」, 「誰」, or 「どこ」, it means “more than any ...” — a superlative.
senses.connection: Question word (「何」, 「誰」) + にもまして
examples: Health is more important than anything.
He has worked harder than anyone.

notes: The first item must be something that is already high in degree: last year was already hot, so you can say 「今年は去年にもまして暑い」. If last year was cool, say 「今年は去年よりずっと暑い」; 「にもまして」 would be wrong.
「何にもまして」 and 「誰にもまして」 mean “more than anything / anyone”, a superlative. After the question word 「も」 is required: ✕「何にまして」→ ○「何にもまして」.

daily.title: Worried about a friend
daily.description: Noticing a friend doesn't look well today.
daily.example: What's wrong? You look even paler than usual.

daily.title: Talking about the season
daily.description: Chatting with a neighbor about hay fever this year.
daily.example: There's even more pollen this year than last year, isn't there?

work.title: New Year's speech
work.description: The company president sets expectations in a New Year's address.
work.example: This year will probably be even tougher than last year.

work.title: Stressing priorities
work.description: Stressing safety first at a safety meeting.
work.example: Above all else, please put employee safety first.

etymology: 「まして」 is the te-form of the verb 「増す (ます)」, meaning “to increase, to grow”. 「AにもましてB」 literally means “B, increasing even beyond A”.

similar.title: 〜以上に
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「以上に」 means exceeding some standard or expectation (「予想以上に難しい」) and does not assume the standard itself is high; 「にもまして」 stresses that the first item is already high and the second surpasses it, in a more literary style.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Both compare. 「より」 is an ordinary comparison and does not assume the first item is high; 「にもまして」 implies the first item is already quite remarkable.

formation: It is built from the particle 「に」 (the standard of comparison) + 「も」 (“even”, first admitting that the first item is already so) + 「まして」 (the te-form of 「増す」, to increase). 「Aにもまして」 literally means “even compared with A, it has increased a further level”. 「も」 first affirms A as “already high”, and 「増して」 adds more, so “A is already ..., B is even more ...”. When the first item is 「何」, 「誰」 or 「いつ」, it becomes “more than any ...”, a superlative (「いつにもまして」 = more than usual).

meaning: Shows a state or feeling at its peak, “utmost ...”. Mostly used in formal greetings. 「若気の至り」 means “a result of youthful recklessness”.

senses.label: The utmost ...
senses.meaning: Shows a feeling at its peak, used in formal thanks or apologies. These are fixed phrases; common ones are 「光栄の至り」, 「恐縮の至り」, and 「感激の至り」.
senses.connection: 「光栄」, 「恐縮」, 「感激」, 「赤面」, etc. + の至りです
examples: It is the greatest honor to receive such an award.
I am truly grateful that you took the time to come despite your busy schedule.

senses.label: Youthful recklessness
senses.meaning: 「若気の至り」 is a set phrase meaning “(a mistake made) out of youthful impulsiveness”. Often used when looking back on your own past failures.
senses.connection: 若気の至り(で)
examples: That was youthful recklessness — I'm embarrassed when I think about it now.
Please laugh off my mistakes from my student days as youthful folly.

notes: 「光栄の至り」 and 「恐縮の至り」 are only for your own feelings (gratitude, humility), not for the other person: ✕「先生は光栄の至りでしょう」.
「若気の至り」 is used for your own past mistakes, with a note of excuse and self-mockery; using it to judge someone else (「あなたの若気の至りですね」) sounds condescending, and to an elder it is rude.
The combinations are fixed and cannot be applied freely to other emotions: ✕「悲しみの至り」, 「疲労の至り」→ ○「悲しみの極み」, 「疲労の極み」.
「至らない点も多いですが」 is a humble “I have many shortcomings” and has nothing to do with this grammar; don't read it as “reach”.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Chatting with old classmates about embarrassing things from your youth.
daily.example: Dyeing my hair blond was just youthful folly.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: A character in a novel gives formal thanks.
daily.example: I am deeply moved to receive such hospitality.

work.title: Award speech
work.description: Giving a speech at an awards ceremony.
work.example: I am deeply honored to receive such a prestigious award.

work.title: Business apology
work.description: Apologizing to a client for your own mistake.
work.example: I am thoroughly ashamed to have made such a basic mistake.

etymology: 「至り」 is the noun form of the verb 「至る」 (to reach), meaning “the farthest point reached, the peak”. 「〜の至り」 means “the peak of ...”, hence “utmost ...”. 「若気の至り」 is “the result of youthful impulsiveness at its peak”.

similar.title: 〜の極み
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning; both mean “extreme”. 「の極み」 has a wider use and works for positive and negative (「贅沢の極み」, 「疲労の極み」); 「の至り」 is mostly used in formal greetings and speeches.

similar.title: 〜限りだ
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「限りだ」 attaches to adjectives and shows the speaker's strong feeling right now (「うれしい限りだ」), less formal; 「の至り」 attaches to nouns and is a formal set phrase.

similar.title: 〜極まる／〜極まりない
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「極まる」 mostly follows na-adjective stems and often carries negative judgment (「失礼極まりない」); 「の至り」 is mostly a set phrase for thanks and apologies.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「至る」). 「に至る」 shows a situation reaching some stage (「倒産に至る」); 「の至り」 nominalizes 「至る」 and shows a feeling at its peak.

formation: It is the continuative form 「至り」 of the verb 「至る」 (to reach) turned into a noun, meaning “the very end reached, the extreme”; with 「Aの」 in front it is “the extreme of A”. With 「光栄」, 「恐縮」 or 「感激」, it means that feeling has reached its peak, “extremely ...”. 「若気の至り」 takes the sense “the result of going all the way to the end”: what you did when youthful high spirits ran away with you, i.e. “something done out of youthful folly”. Because the basic meaning is “reaching the peak”, it combines fixedly only with a few feeling nouns that have a degree.

meaning: Means “never mind A — even B (which is more extreme) ...”. Mostly used for negative or surprising situations.
connection: Noun + はおろか (〜も／さえ／まで)

senses.label: Let alone ..., not even ...
senses.meaning: The first part is the obvious level; the second is a more extreme example. Usually with a negative, showing a bad situation. The second part often takes 「も」, 「さえ」, 「すら」, or 「まで」.
senses.connection: Noun + はおろか、Noun + も／さえ／すら + negative
examples: I can't read hiragana, let alone kanji.
I'm so busy that I don't even have time to sleep on my days off, let alone travel.
Because of my injury, I can't even walk, let alone run.

senses.label: Positive use
senses.meaning: Can also be used in positive sentences to show a surprisingly wide range: “not only ..., but even ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + はおろか、Noun + まで／も + positive
examples: His name is known not only in Japan but even overseas.
That shop is never short of customers — not just on weekdays, but even late at night.

notes: Put a light, obvious thing first and a more extreme one after; reverse the order and it makes no sense: ✕「歩くことはおろか、走ることもできない」→ ○「走ることはおろか、歩くこともできない」.
The second part cannot be a command, invitation, intention or request: ✕「漢字はおろか、ひらがなも覚えなさい」→ ○「漢字はもちろん、ひらがなも覚えなさい」.
The second half normally needs 「も」, 「さえ」, 「すら」 or 「まで」 to match; with only 「はおろか」 and none of these, the sentence sounds incomplete.

daily.title: Complaining about pay
daily.description: Telling a friend how tight money is.
daily.example: My pay is so low that I can't even cover my monthly living expenses, let alone save.

daily.title: Talking about your kid
daily.description: A parent worries that their child is hooked on games.
daily.example: My kid plays games without even eating, let alone doing homework.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on the severe situation in a disaster area.
work.example: In the disaster area, even the water supply is still cut off, not to mention the electricity.

work.title: Reporting a problem
work.description: Explaining a project's difficulties to the boss.
work.example: We haven't secured enough staff, let alone the budget.

etymology: 「おろか (愚か)」 originally means “foolish, not worth mentioning”. 「〜はおろか」 meant “it would be foolish even to mention ...”, which came to mean “never mind ...”.

similar.title: 〜どころか
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「どころか」 can also show the exact opposite of what is expected (「痩せるどころか太った」); 「はおろか」 only means “A goes without saying, even B ...”.

similar.title: 〜はもとより
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「はもとより」 is mostly used for positive or neutral things, is milder, and can be used with commands and invitations; 「はおろか」 is mostly for negative situations, with surprise or dissatisfaction.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: The meaning is close, and they are often used together: 「AはおろかBすら〜ない」. 「すら」 brings out the extreme example “even ...”, and 「はおろか」 brushes aside the lighter first item.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「ばかりか」 means “not only ... but also ...” and works for positive and negative; 「はおろか」 stresses the extremeness of the second item and is mostly negative.

formation: It is built from the topic particle 「は」 + the stem of the na-adjective 「おろか（愚か）」 (foolish, not worth mentioning). 「Aはおろか」 literally means “As for A, (even mentioning it) is foolish”: A is so obvious that it needs no discussion. The speaker brushes A aside and then uses 「も」, 「さえ」 or 「すら」 to bring in the more extreme B, creating the build-up “A goes without saying, even B ...”. Since “even mentioning A is superfluous” is itself exaggerated, the sentence often carries surprise or dissatisfaction.

meaning: Stresses “precisely because ...”, highlighting the reason. Usually a positive or well-meaning reason.
connection: Verb / adjective conditional form (〜ば) + こそ

senses.label: Precisely because ...
senses.meaning: Stresses that the first part is the one true reason. Often used to explain that something that looks bad is actually well-meant. Formal; common in writing and speeches.
senses.connection: Verb ば-form / い-adjective 〜ければ / な-adjective・noun 〜であれば + こそ
examples: It's precisely because I care about you that I'm being so strict.
It's precisely because you're healthy that you can enjoy your work.
Because I have my family, I can keep going no matter how hard it gets.

senses.label: At the end of a sentence
senses.meaning: End the sentence with 「〜ばこそだ／ばこそです」 to mean “it's all because of ...”. Often used to thank people.
senses.connection: 〜のも、〜ばこそだ／ばこそです
examples: I owe getting this far entirely to everyone's support.
Parents are strict precisely because they love their children.

senses.label: No room at all
senses.meaning: The old phrase 「〜もあらばこそ」 means “there wasn't even a chance to ...”. Only found in fixed phrases and literature.
senses.connection: Noun + もあらばこそ (e.g. 「止める間もあらばこそ」)
examples: Before anyone could stop him, he dashed outside.

notes: The reasons are mostly positive motives such as care, concern, trust or effort, often explaining that “being strict is actually for your sake”. With a purely negative cause it sounds unnatural: ✕「怠けていればこそ失敗した」→ ○「怠けていたから失敗した」.
It must attach to the 「ば」 form, unlike 「からこそ」: ✕「思うばこそ」→ ○「思えばこそ」; for nouns and na-adjectives use 「であればこそ」.
「止める間もあらばこそ」 and 「〜もあらばこそ」 are the classical rhetorical use, meaning “there was no (room for) ...”, the opposite of “precisely because”. Watch out when reading.

daily.title: A parent explains
daily.description: A mother tells her child why she scolded him.
daily.example: Mom gets angry precisely because she cares about you so much.

daily.title: Seen in a novel
daily.description: A character thinks back on why he kept going.
daily.example: It's only because you were here that I made it this far.

work.title: Thank-you speech
work.description: Thanking coworkers at retirement.
work.example: I owe my long career here entirely to all of your support.

work.title: A boss gives guidance
work.description: A boss explains why he is so demanding.
work.example: It's precisely because I expect a lot from you that I'm telling you these hard truths.

etymology: Made of the conditional particle 「ば」 and the emphasis particle 「こそ」. In classical Japanese, the realis form (izenkei) + 「ば」 expressed a definite cause (“because ...”), and adding 「こそ」 made it “precisely because ...”. 「あらばこそ」 keeps an old ironic use from classical Japanese.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning, and it also uses 「こそ」. 「からこそ」 is more colloquial, widely used, and can also give negative causes; 「ばこそ」 is more literary and mostly used for positive, well-meant reasons.

similar.title: 〜てこそ
similar.explanation: It is also built with 「こそ」. 「てこそ」 means “only if ... can ...” and stresses the condition (「努力してこそ」); 「ばこそ」 stresses the reason.

similar.title: 〜こそ
similar.explanation: Same origin (the 「こそ」 in 「ばこそ」 is this one). 「こそ」 alone follows a noun for emphasis (「今こそ」); 「ばこそ」 is a fixed combination that stresses a reason.

formation: It is built from the conditional particle 「ば」 + the emphatic particle 「こそ」. In classical Japanese 「realis form＋ば」 expressed an established reason (“because ...”), and the modern 「ば」 form takes over that use here; with the exclusive emphasis of 「こそ」 added, it becomes “precisely because ... (and not anything else)”, pinning down the one reason more strongly than 「から」. As for 「あらばこそ」, 「あら」 is the irrealis form, and 「irrealis＋ば」 is hypothetical; with 「こそ」 it forms a strong rhetorical “how could there be”, so the meaning is “there was none at all”.

meaning: Shows that once something happens, it's all over and every effort is wasted. Also used for “if you put it that way, there's nothing more to say”.
connection: Verb ば-form / たら-form + それまでだ

senses.label: Once ..., it's all over
senses.meaning: If the first situation happens, everything before it loses its meaning. Sounds resigned or warning. Often used with 「〜てしまえば」 or 「いくら〜ても」.
senses.connection: Verb ば-form / たら-form + それまでだ (often 「〜てしまえばそれまでだ」)
examples: No matter how much money you save, once you die, that's the end of it.
Even the most expensive machine is useless once it breaks.
All that preparation goes to waste if it rains on the day.

senses.label: Nothing more to say
senses.meaning: 「〜と言われればそれまでだが」 means “if someone says that, there's no arguing with it”. Usually followed by your own opinion.
senses.connection: 〜と言われれば／言ってしまえば + それまでだが、〜
examples: If you say I was just lucky, I can't argue, but I think I worked hard too.
You could just call it a matter of taste, but I think this one is better.

notes: Here 「それまで」 means “that's the end of everything”, not “until then”: 「死んでしまえばそれまでだ」 is “once you die, that's it”.

「〜と言われればそれまでだが、…」 is a set phrase that first concedes the other's point and then politely holds your own view; it softens a rebuttal nicely in meetings. If you say only the first half, 「〜と言われればそれまでです」, it means “then I have nothing to say” and sounds sulky or like giving up.
Don't confuse it with 「までだ」: 「やるまでだ」 follows the dictionary form and shows resolve, “I'll just do it”; 「ばそれまでだ」 must follow the conditional 「ば／たら」: ✕「失敗するそれまでだ」→ ○「失敗すればそれまでだ」.

daily.title: Urging a friend to back up
daily.description: A friend has lots of photos on their phone but no backup.
daily.example: If you lose your phone, they're all gone. Make sure you back them up.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Telling a family member not to overwork.
daily.example: If you ruin your health, it's all over, so don't push yourself.

work.title: Stressing safety
work.description: A supervisor reminds workers about safety at a construction site.
work.example: No matter how well we keep to the schedule, one accident and it's all over.

work.title: Discussing a plan
work.description: Acknowledging someone's view in a meeting, then giving your own.
work.example: You could say it's just a cost issue, but quality matters too.

etymology: 「それまで」 literally means “up to that point”. 「〜ばそれまでだ」 means “if ..., things end right there”, which came to mean that everything is over and can't be undone.

similar.title: 〜が最後／〜たら最後
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「たら最後」 means “once ..., it inevitably leads to a bad result”, and that result must be stated (「寝たら最後、朝まで起きない」); 「ばそれまでだ」 simply says “it's all over”.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: The meaning is close, and both suggest “futile even if done”. 「たところで」 means “even if you do ..., (it's no use)” and is followed by a negative result; 「ばそれまでだ」 means “once ... happens, it's all over”, where the first part is the event that wipes everything out.

similar.title: 〜ても始まらない
similar.explanation: The meaning is close. 「ても始まらない」 means “it's too late now, ... won't help” (「後悔しても始まらない」) and targets an action; 「ばそれまでだ」 targets a situation that, once it occurs, cannot be undone.

similar.title: 〜までだ／〜までのことだ
similar.explanation: Both use 「まで」, but the meaning differs. 「までだ」 follows a dictionary-form verb and means “at worst I'll just ...” (「だめならやり直すまでだ」), expressing resolve; 「ばそれまでだ」 means “once ..., it's over”.

formation: It is built from the conditional 「〜ば／〜たら」 + 「それまで」 (up to that point) + the copula 「だ」. 「それ」 points to the moment the preceding condition is met, 「まで」 marks the end point, so 「それまでだ」 means “things end at that moment”. Thus 「Aばそれまでだ」 means “once A happens, everything ends there”: all the effort and accumulation before it go back to zero. 「〜と言われればそれまでだ」 treats the discussion itself as that event: once the other person says that, the discussion is over, i.e. “if they put it like that, there's nothing more to say”.
